title: Scythia, as medieval writers used it
fact_summary: When the Hungarians appeared, Regino of Prüm described them by copying an ancient Roman account of the Scythians. The label says more about his books than about the Hungarians.

claims.text: Under 889 Regino begins: “Scythia, ut aiunt, in oriente extensa”, Scythia, so they say, stretches to the east, bounded by the Pontus, the Riphean mountains, Asia and the river Ithasis.
claims.certainty_reason: This records what the source says. The passage was read in Latin in the open copy linked under Sources.

claims.text: He describes the Scythians as herders without houses who carry wives and children in wagons, live on milk and honey, and dress in animal skins.
claims.certainty_reason: This records what the source says. The passage was read in Latin in the open copy linked under Sources.

claims.text: He credits them with driving out the Persian king Darius and killing Cyrus with his whole army.
claims.certainty_reason: This records what the source says. The passage was read in Latin in the open copy linked under Sources.

claims.text: Regino took this description from Justin's Epitome, an ancient Roman work, and used it to describe the Hungarians.

held_by.who: The editors of the Mapping Medieval Peoples database

claims.certainty_reason: A note in the database. Justin's text has not been opened to compare the wording.

open_questions.text: How much of what Regino says about the Hungarians comes from what he heard, and how much from old books?
